newsitem.title: UK: Pearson accounting problem at Penguin.
newsitem.headline: Pearson accounting problem at Penguin.

text.p: British media group Pearson Plc said Thursday that improper accounting at its Penguin USA books unit would force it to take a charge of up to 100 million pounds ($163 million) against 1996 profits.

Pearson said the problems, which date back to 1991 but emerged only very recently, arose from unauthorised discounting of invoices for early payment by customers, with the discounts not fully recognised in Penguin USA's accounts.
The news of the charge, which one analyst called "quite a horrific provision," initially sent Pearson shares into a tailspin.

The complex nature of publishers' accounts, with hundreds of thousands of transactions passing through the New-York based Penguin USA's New Jersey facility, where its accounting operations are, made it easier for a what a Pearson spokesman called a "very determined individual" to conceal the discrepancies.

"I think we are dealing with a very determined individual," the spokesman said. "We are confident we have provided for not only what we have discovered so far but also what will be discovered (as the investigation continues to its conclusion)," the spokesman said.
Pearson said that those found to be responsible for the problem, "have been and will be appropriately dealt with," without giving details.

Marjorie Scardino, who took over as Pearson chief executive at the start of the year, said in the statement, "We have moved quickly to implement a detailed plan of action to address these unauthorised practices."

De Larrinaga said the news showed Scardino and her new team were "tightening up," but said it highlighted the problems she faces in tackling Pearson's woes, as well as asking serious questions of management controls.

The problems were uncovered by Michael Lynton, who took over as Penguin chairman and chief executive in January, and his management team, and are being investigated by lawyers and by accountants Price Waterhouse.
Pearson said the profits of Penguin would not be restated and Pearson has not changed its 1997 profit expectations for the company as a result of the unauthorised discounts.
The scale of the provisions compare with 1996 gross sales at Penguin USA -- before allowances for books returned -- of 300 million pounds ($489.6 million).
Scardino, a Texan who came to the top job at Pearson from its 50-percent owned Economist magazine business, has said that Pearson's profit performance is not good enough.

Pearson is due to announce its 1996 results on March 18. Pre-tax profits, before the Penguin USA provision, are forecast at between 235 million and 290 million pounds ($383 million and $473 million), down from 365.1 million ($596 million) in 1995.
